Measuring and comparing configurations

Source: vignettes/evaluate.Rmd
evaluate.Rmd

Every choice in a pipeline (the recipe, the model, the prompt, the reasoning effort) changes the answers, and one run on one document cannot tell you by how much. A model asked the same question five times can answer it five ways. Ten questions about one report share that report’s quirks, so they are closer to one observation than to ten.

gr_compare() shows what each recipe does to one document, and its output is descriptive only. With the functions in this guide you answer the next question: on a labelled set of questions, is configuration A more accurate than B, by how much, at what cost, and how sure can you be?

The sections follow the order of the work: a reference set and its splits, the arms to compare and the rule that scores them, a benchmark held to one spending limit, the report and how to read it, planning the size of a comparison before you run it, judges, baselines that use no model, drift, and the signals the package records about its own work. The statistics functions underneath come last. Measuring a screener against people, several reviewers and agreement between extraction tables belong to a review, so vignette("review") covers them. vignette("compare") puts these functions to work on worked comparisons of readers, segmenters, settings, screening and judges.

Setting up

Every example runs offline. hr_mock_client() stands in for the model, and embedder = "lexical" keeps retrieval free and deterministic. The setup gives two mock model ids prices, so the benchmarks below have a cost to compare: mock-small at $0.20 and $0.80 per million input and output tokens, and mock-large at ten times that.

library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

hr_register_model("mock-small", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 0.2, output_usd = 0.8)
hr_register_model("mock-large", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)

References and splits

A reference is the labelled set you score every configuration on. Each item has a payload (what the configuration is given), a label (what counts as right), a cluster and a split. The cluster is the unit whose items share errors, usually the document. Eight questions about one report are not eight independent observations, and every interval in this guide is computed with that in mind. hr_reference() builds a reference from any items. gr_qa_reference() builds one from questions about documents, with each question’s acceptable answers:

reports <- c(
  north = "The northern region. Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024. The plant in Leeds made 12,400 units.",
  south = "The southern region. Revenue was 51.8 million dollars in fiscal 2025. Staff numbered 310 at year end.",
  east  = "The eastern region. Revenue was 38.9 million dollars in fiscal 2024. The chair is Ana Ruiz.",
  west  = "The western region. Revenue was 29.4 million dollars in fiscal 2023. Exports rose 7 percent.")

qa <- gr_qa_reference(
  questions = c(n_rev = "What was revenue?", n_units = "How many units did Leeds make?",
                s_rev = "What was revenue?", s_staff = "How many staff were there?",
                e_rev = "What was revenue?", e_ceo = "Who is the chief executive?",
                w_rev = "What was revenue?", w_exp = "By how much did exports rise?"),
  documents = rep(unname(reports), each = 2),
  answers = list("45.2 million", c("12,400", "12400"), "51.8 million", "310",
                 "38.9 million", NA, "29.4 million", "7 percent"),
  unanswerable = "e_ceo",
  cluster = rep(names(reports), each = 2),
  split = "test")
qa
#> <hr_reference> 8 item(s) in 4 cluster(s)
#>   splits: test 8 
#>   hash: d64da50d3779

The eastern report names a chair and no chief executive, so e_ceo is marked unanswerable. Its label is the not-found answer, and a reader is right on it only when it says the document does not hold the answer. The flag goes into the label alone. The payload holds the question and the document, so a configuration cannot tell which questions have no answer. Without such items, a reference never tests whether a reader can tell that an answer is missing.

An item with neither an answer nor the unanswerable flag has no label. Every run on it is scored NA, so it never counts for or against an arm.

A benchmark locks a reference once it starts scoring it. From then on hr_reference_add() refuses to add items to the reference, or to any copy of it, with an error of class hr_reference_locked, so no one can add an item after seeing the results. The reference also carries a SHA-256 hash of its content, and the benchmark checks that hash.

Splits keep tuning apart from evidence:

  • dev is for tuning prompts, settings and margins, and its scores are never reported.
  • exploratory holds early experiments.
  • calibration is for fitting signal thresholds (below).
  • test holds the items reported comparisons are scored on.
  • final, if used, is held back and run once per release.

hr_assign_splits() assigns whole clusters, so no document has questions on both sides of a tuning and a scoring split:

questions <- data.frame(
  item_id  = sprintf("q%03d", 1:120),
  document = rep(sprintf("report%02d.pdf", 1:30), each = 4),
  question = rep(c("What was revenue?", "Who audited the accounts?",
                   "How many staff were there?", "When did the year end?"), 30))
sp <- hr_assign_splits(questions, seed = 2026)
sp
#> <hr_splits> 120 item(s) in 30 cluster(s), method stable, seed 2026
#> 
#>        split target clusters items cluster_share item_share
#>          dev    0.1        4    16         0.133      0.133
#>  exploratory    0.1        3    12         0.100      0.100
#>  calibration    0.3       10    40         0.333      0.333
#>         test    0.5       13    52         0.433      0.433

The default shares are 10% dev, 10% exploratory, 30% calibration and 50% test. The SHA-256 digest of the seed and a cluster’s id sets that cluster’s split, so row order and the session’s random state do not change it. With the default method = "stable", adding or dropping a document never moves another. In exchange, the shares hold only on average: 13 of these 30 documents went to test, not 15.

method = "balanced" gives each split its share of whole clusters. A document added later can then shift others across a boundary, so draw the splits once and store them:

hr_assign_splits(questions, seed = 2026, method = "balanced")$counts[, c("split", "clusters", "items")]
#>         split clusters items
#> 1         dev        3    12
#> 2 exploratory        3    12
#> 3 calibration        9    36
#> 4        test       15    60

With very few documents, a split given a share can receive no cluster, and hr_assign_splits() then warns with class hr_empty_split.

Label sheets

Labels come from people. gr_label_sheet() writes a CSV with one row per item, the columns a person needs to judge it and empty columns for their decisions, plus an instructions file beside it. It writes six kinds: "qa", "screening", "extraction", "calibration", "judge" and "pairwise" (two texts in a blinded order, for a pairwise judge; vignette("compare") has one). Sheets are blind by default: a blind sheet copies only those columns, so a model’s answer in items stays out of it:

to_label <- head(sp$items, 3)
to_label$model_answer <- c("45.2 million", "Not stated", "310")

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "qa-labels.csv")
sheet <- gr_label_sheet("qa", to_label, path = path)
names(sheet)
#> [1] "item_id"    "document"   "question"   "answerable" "answer"    
#> [6] "quote"      "note"

The person fills answerable, answer and quote. gr_read_labels() reads the sheet back, checks every value and id, and joins the items’ other columns by item_id. It renames a column that clashes with a decision column, so a model’s answer here would come back as model_answer:

filled <- read.csv(path, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
filled$answerable <- c("yes", "no", "yes")
filled$answer <- c("45.2 million dollars", NA, "310")
write.csv(filled, path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")

gr_read_labels(path, "qa", items = to_label)[, c("item_id", "answerable", "answer",
                                                  "split", "model_answer")]
#>   item_id answerable               answer split model_answer
#> 1    q001       TRUE 45.2 million dollars   dev 45.2 million
#> 2    q002      FALSE                 <NA>   dev   Not stated
#> 3    q003       TRUE                  310   dev          310

A value it cannot read stops it with an error of class gr_bad_labels. The error lists every bad value at once, each with the sheet, the row number as a spreadsheet counts it, and the item:

filled$answer[2] <- "Smith & Co"
write.csv(filled, path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
tryCatch(gr_read_labels(path, "qa", items = to_label),
         gr_bad_labels = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e)))
#> 1 value(s) in the qa sheet cannot be read:
#> qa-labels.csv row 3 (item 'q002'): `answerable` is no but `answer` is filled; clear one of them.

With reviewers = k, each person gets a sheet of their own and sees no one else’s decisions. ?gr_label_sheet gives the number of items each kind of set needs for the package’s own evaluation: about 480 questions over 88 documents for question answering.

Arms and scorers

An arm is one configuration to compare: a function of an item and a context that returns the arm’s output for that item. ctx carries the benchmark’s client, a trace of this run alone, the governor the run is held to and the run’s draw_index. ctx$call() is hr_call() with the client, the trace and the draw index filled in. Send every request an arm makes through that trace: the benchmark counts the run’s tokens and dollars there and holds the run to the limit through it:

ask <- function(name, model) {
  hr_arm(name, function(item, ctx) {
    ctx$call(paste("Item", item), model = ctx$params$model)$text
  }, params = list(model = model))
}
ask("large", "mock-large")
#> <hr_arm large> version 0.0.1
#>   params: model = mock-large 
#>   hash: 4a659e23a5b4

The arm records a SHA-256 hash of its name, code, settings and version. The hash covers the code as text plus the values it names from the environment it was made in, the workspace included. An arm written at top level that reads a global prompt therefore gets a new hash when the prompt changes. The same arm has the same hash in every session and after saveRDS(). hr_benchmark() refuses an arm edited after it was built instead of running it under its old name. Change version when the arm’s behaviour changes.

gr_arm() wraps a reading recipe as an arm, and gr_arms() builds one per recipe. Each run reads the item’s document with answer_document(), or with gr_read() when the document is already chunked, and returns the gr_answer. settings takes what answer_document() takes in .... Here the settings make one recipe into two arms on two models:

arms <- list(gr_arm("fast", settings = list(model = "mock-small"), name = "small"),
             gr_arm("fast", settings = list(model = "mock-large"), name = "large"))

A gr_arm() takes the package version as its version, since readers and prompts change between releases. Every request of a run carries the run’s draw index, segmenter and reader requests included. If the run’s limits leave a reader too little room to start, the reader returns a partial not-found answer that notes the limit, and that answer is scored as a budget stop, not an error.

A scorer turns an output and a label into correct, an outcome (what it compared) and a failure_kind saying why a wrong output was wrong: "parse_failure", "refusal", "not_in_document", "wrong", "budget_stop" or "error". hr_scorer_exact(), the default, compares text after folding case and white space. For reading recipes, use gr_scorer_answer(). It counts an answer right when the answer contains any acceptable answer, after folding case, white space and thousands separators. Numbers are matched whole: "12" is not found in ".12" or "-12", but is found in "12-15", and "45.2" in "45.2m":

s <- gr_scorer_answer()
item <- list(question = "How many units?", document = gr_example())
s$fn(item, "Leeds made 12,400 units.", "12400")$correct
#> [1] TRUE
s$fn(item, "Leeds made 112,400 units.", "12400")$correct
#> [1] FALSE
s$fn(item, "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", "12400")$failure_kind
#> [1] "wrong"

On an unanswerable item it counts an answer right when is_not_found() is TRUE and no limit or refusal stopped the run, since a reader that ran out of budget did not look. To write your own scorer, pass a function of (item, output, label) to hr_scorer(); its help has one that accepts a number within 1% of the label.

Running a benchmark

hr_benchmark() runs every arm on every item of the chosen splits runs times, scores each output, and returns one row per cluster, item, arm and run. The stand-in model below knows each report’s facts. Asked as mock-small, it replies that the report is unclear on 30% of requests; asked as mock-large, it never does:

facts <- list(
  northern = c(revenue = "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", units = "Leeds made 12,400 units."),
  southern = c(revenue = "Revenue was 51.8 million dollars.", staff = "There were 310 staff."),
  eastern  = c(revenue = "Revenue was 38.9 million dollars."),
  western  = c(revenue = "Revenue was 29.4 million dollars.", exports = "Exports rose 7 percent."))

cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  seen <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), ""), collapse = " ")
  region <- regmatches(seen, regexpr("(northern|southern|eastern|western)", seen))
  asked <- sub(".*Question", "", seen)
  topic <- c("revenue", "units", "staff", "exports")
  hit <- topic[vapply(topic, grepl, logical(1), x = asked, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
  reply <- facts[[region]][hit]
  if (is.na(reply)) return("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT")
  if (identical(params$model, "mock-small") && runif(1) < 0.3) return("The report is unclear.")
  reply
})

bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
bench
#> <hr_bench> 2 arm(s) x 8 item(s) in 4 cluster(s) x 5 run(s); split test; scorer answer_contains
#>  arm   accuracy runs wrong failed budget_stop usd   
#>  small 0.750    40   10    0      0           0.0013
#>  large 1.000    40    0    0      0           0.0132
#>   Descriptive only: accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over labelled items, with no interval.
head(bench[, c("item", "arm", "run", "correct", "failure_kind", "usd", "draw_index")])
#>    item   arm run correct failure_kind      usd draw_index
#> 1 n_rev small   1   FALSE        wrong 3.10e-05          1
#> 2 n_rev small   2    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-05          2
#> 3 n_rev small   3    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-05          3
#> 4 n_rev small   4    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-05          4
#> 5 n_rev small   5   FALSE        wrong 3.10e-05          5
#> 6 n_rev large   1    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-04          1

The printed accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over items. It is descriptive and has no interval. The arms run under a private random stream started from seed (1 by default), so the mock’s runif() gives the same draws every time this guide is built, and the caller’s random state is left as it was. Rows on the dev split are marked reportable = FALSE and printed apart.

Five runs is the default and the expected minimum. Fewer warns with class hr_few_runs, because with fewer runs you cannot tell the spread from run to run apart from the difference between arms.

One limit for the whole benchmark

The whole benchmark is one run under one hr_governor(). Each run’s trace is held to the governor’s limits less what the runs before it used, so the limit you set is the most the whole comparison can spend. With governor = NULL the limits come from hr_options(), and its default of 400 calls is easy to exceed: two arms on 300 items for 5 runs make 3000 calls. A run stopped by a refused request is recorded as a "budget_stop" and counted wrong. The runs after it still start, so every row exists and you can see the refusals:

capitals <- hr_reference(items = list(q1 = "France", q2 = "Peru", q3 = "Chad", q4 = "Fiji"),
                         labels = c("Paris", "Lima", "N'Djamena", "Suva"),
                         cluster = c("a", "a", "b", "b"), split = "test")
atlas <- c(France = "Paris", Peru = "Lima", Chad = "N'Djamena", Fiji = "Suva")
geo <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) atlas[[sub("Capital of ", "", messages[[1]]$content)]])
capital <- hr_arm("capital", function(item, ctx) ctx$call(paste0("Capital of ", item))$text)

short <- hr_benchmark(capital, capitals, runs = 5, client = geo,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 6))
#> Warning in warn_budget_stops(out, stop_limit, governor, from_options): 14 of 20
#> runs were stopped by the benchmark's limits (calls: 14). All of them are
#> counted wrong in the accuracy, intervals and comparisons. The first was item
#> 'q2', arm 'capital', run 2.
table(short$failure_kind, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> budget_stop        <NA> 
#>          14           6

The first six runs got answers. The governor refused the other fourteen before anything was sent. Whenever a limit stops a run, hr_benchmark() warns with class hr_budget_stopped and gives the number stopped, the limit that stopped them, how many of them count against an arm and the first run stopped. When the limits came from hr_options(), the warning gives the values of the options that stopped runs and says to pass a governor sized for the benchmark.

Repeated runs must be repeated draws

Run r gets ctx$draw_index = r, and its ctx$trace carries r, so ctx$call() and every stage called with trace = ctx$trace send their requests at the run’s draw. Under an hr_cache() each run is its own cache entry, and under an hr_replay_client() its own recorded draw. The recorded draw also names the arm, so a replay answers each arm with its own replies, whether it replays every arm or a few, in any order.

Five runs answered from one stored reply would agree perfectly and measure nothing. hr_benchmark() therefore refuses an arm whose runs come back as copies, with an error of class hr_duplicate_draw. An arm that sends every run’s request at one fixed draw index is such an arm:

cache <- hr_cache()
cached <- hr_cache_client(geo, cache)
invisible(hr_benchmark(capital, capitals, runs = 5, client = cached))

fixed_draw <- hr_arm("fixed_draw", function(item, ctx) {
  hr_call(ctx$client, paste0("Capital of ", item), trace = ctx$trace,
          draw_index = 1)$text
})
tryCatch(hr_benchmark(fixed_draw, capitals, runs = 5, client = cached),
         hr_duplicate_draw = function(e) class(e)[1])
#> [1] "hr_duplicate_draw"

A cache still saves requests. Run the capital benchmark again under the same cache and it sends no request and costs nothing, since each run is answered from its own entry. An hr_mock_client() keeps no cache, so under it the fixed_draw arm is not refused; under a cache it is.

Reading the report

hr_report() turns the reportable rows into accuracy per arm with intervals that keep clusters together, paired differences, stability, reliability, cost and failures. B sets the number of cluster bootstrap resamples, 2000 by default. This guide uses fewer so it builds quickly.

rpt <- hr_report(bench, B = 200)
rpt
#> <hr_bench_report> 2 arm(s), 8 item(s) in 4 cluster(s), 5 run(s)
#> Intervals: cluster-robust t on the logit scale, C - 1 df at 95% (8 items in 4 clusters fall short of 300 items and 30 clusters).
#> 
#> Accuracy (arms in benchmark order, not ranked):
#>  arm   accuracy interval       rank_interval
#>  small 0.750    [0.648, 0.830] 2-2          
#>  large 1.000    [0.561, 1.000] 1-1          
#> 
#> Paired differences (first minus second):
#>  contrast      difference interval         simultaneous    
#>  small - large -0.250     [-0.342, -0.158] [-0.342, -0.158]
#> 
#> Stability across runs:
#>  arm   flip_rate TARa  run_sd
#>  small 0.750     0.250 0.153 
#>  large 0.000     1.000 0.000 
#> 
#> Reliability:
#>  arm   pass^1 pass^3 pass^5
#>  small 0.750  0.425  0.250 
#>  large 1.000  1.000  1.000 
#> 
#> Cost:
#>  arm   usd_per_item usd_per_correct interval               tokens_per_item
#>  small 3.24e-05     4.32e-05        [3.946e-05, 4.733e-05] 127.9          
#>  large 0.000331     0.000331        [0.0003192, 0.0003405] 128.8          
#>  estimated       on_frontier frontier_share
#>  100.000% (flag) yes         1.000         
#>  100.000% (flag) yes         1.000         
#> 
#> Failures (all counted wrong):
#>  arm   wrong without_parse_refusal
#>  small 10    0.750                
#>  large  0    1.000                
#> 
#> Variance on the probability scale: within-item runs 0.075, between items 0.019, within share 0.800.
#> Note: More than 5% of the cost of small, large rests on estimated token counts; read its cost as approximate. 
#> Note: Run-to-run variance is 80% of the total, above 10%: use runs = 10. 
#> Note: Cost, pass^k, frontier share and rank intervals come from the cluster bootstrap, which can undercover below 300 items or 30 clusters; read them as rough. 
#> Note: Accuracy of large is 0, 1 or the same in every cluster, where the t interval is not defined; its interval is Korn and Graubard's, one-sided from 0 or 1 at those bounds. 
#> Note: The frontier share (how often an arm is on the cost-accuracy frontier over resamples) is an extension, not a published standard.

With method = "auto", hr_report() picks the interval from the size of the benchmark, and the second line of the print names it and says why. With at least 300 items and at least 30 clusters, method = "auto" uses a studentised cluster bootstrap: each resample draws whole clusters with all their items, runs and arms. Below either threshold, as here, it uses a cluster-robust t interval on the logit scale, with t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom for C clusters.

Neither interval is defined when accuracy is 0 or 1 or the same in every cluster. The arm then gets Korn and Graubard’s interval, one-sided from that bound, and a note says so. That is why large reads [0.561, 1.000] with four clusters behind it. No interval treats items or runs as independent trials. method = "exact" (Clopper-Pearson on the effective number of items) and method = "bayes" (a beta-binomial model with a cluster random effect) are there on request.

These defaults come from simulation. In dev/sim-coverage.R (2000 replicates) the studentised bootstrap covered 95.5% and 95.0% with 386 items in 40 clusters, where the BCa bootstrap it replaced covered 93.5%. The cluster-robust t interval covered 95.7% and 95.8% with 50 items in 10 clusters. The workflow validation.yaml reruns that simulation, and the one behind hr_mdd(), every night.

Paired differences are taken item by item, so each one compares the arms on the same question. Each difference gets a cluster-robust t interval at every size, with simultaneous intervals over all pairs beside it. The report lists arms in benchmark order and does not rank them. The rank interval shows how much the order could change over resamples: small and large here rank 2 and 1 in every one.

The stability rows compare each arm with itself:

  • the flip rate is the share of items whose correctness changed between runs;
  • TARa is the share whose scored output was the same on every run;
  • run_sd is the spread of whole-run accuracy.

small flips on 75% of its items, and an accuracy of 0.750 alone would hide that. Reliability is pass^k, the chance that k runs drawn from an item’s runs are all right, estimated without bias. Here an arm right 75% of the time is right on all five runs of an item only 25% of the time.

Cost comes in dollars and tokens per item and per correct item, since a cheap arm that is often wrong can cost more per right answer than it looks. The report flags an arm when more than 5% of its spend rests on estimated token counts. The mock reports no token counts, so both arms are flagged here. The frontier is the set of arms no other arm beats on both dollars per item and accuracy, with each arm’s share of resamples on it.

Failures are counted by kind, and every one counts as wrong. Beside them, the report gives accuracy recomputed without parse failures and refusals. The variance line splits the spread into within-item (run to run) and between-item parts. When runs account for more than 10% of it, as here at 80%, the report says to use 10 runs.

With fewer than 5 runs the report is descriptive only: point estimates and no intervals. The report refuses an item scored on some runs and not others. The returned list holds every part (rpt$accuracy, rpt$contrasts, rpt$pass_k, rpt$cost, rpt$frontier, rpt$failures, rpt$variance, rpt$notes), and as_json() writes it out.

Errors the arms share

What it controls. hr_error_correlation() measures how far the arms’ errors go together. It gives the phi coefficient between each pair’s errors within strata of item difficulty (n_strata, or your own strata), the share of items both got wrong where they gave the same wrong answer, and a sample of n_check items every arm got wrong, for a person to read. Two arms with good accuracy that fail on the same items gain little from being combined, or from checking each other. The function reads the benchmark’s rows (with held_out = TRUE, only those that count as evidence) and sends nothing. It does not compute Yen’s Q3, the residual correlation of an item response model, since that needs a mixed-model package harnessr does not depend on.

Signs it needs reading. A plan to vote across arms, to use one arm to check another, or to call two arms’ agreement a sign of being right; or a benchmark where most errors fall on a few items.

Where the defaults came from. Three difficulty strata, a sample of ten and reading only held-out rows were set when the metric was added and have not been compared. strata = NULL reads difficulty from the same runs, and seed only makes the hand-check sample repeatable. All five are untested.

How to test it. Here three arms share a blind spot on the first three items and each also fails items of its own, built with hr_sweep():

truth <- hr_reference(sprintf("q%02d", 1:12), labels = rep("yes", 12),
                      cluster = sprintf("c%02d", 1:12), split = "test")
blind <- function(every) {
  hr_arm(paste0("every-", every), function(item, ctx) {
    n <- as.integer(sub("q", "", item))
    if (n <= 3 || n %% every == 0) "no" else "yes"
  }, params = list(every = every))
}
eb <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(blind, list(every = c(4, 5, 6))), truth, runs = 5,
                   client = NULL)
ec <- hr_error_correlation(eb, n_strata = 1)
ec$pairs[, c("arm_a", "arm_b", "phi_pooled", "both_wrong", "same_wrong_rate")]
#>             arm_a           arm_b phi_pooled both_wrong same_wrong_rate
#> 1 every-4:every=4 every-5:every=5  0.1690309          3               1
#> 2 every-4:every=4 every-6:every=6  0.5070926          4               1
#> 3 every-5:every=5 every-6:every=6  0.3142857          3               1
ec$check
#>   item every-4:every=4 every-5:every=5 every-6:every=6
#> 1  q01              no              no              no
#> 2  q02              no              no              no
#> 3  q03              no              no              no

Every pair is positively correlated, and every pair that is wrong together gives the same wrong answer, “no”. Most of that comes from the three items every arm gets wrong. With difficulty strata (n_strata = 3, the default), the function cuts the items by the share of runs that got them wrong:

ec3 <- hr_error_correlation(eb)
table(ec3$strata)
#> 
#> 1 3 
#> 8 4
ec3$phi[, c("arm_a", "arm_b", "stratum", "items", "both_wrong", "phi")]
#>             arm_a           arm_b stratum items both_wrong        phi
#> 1 every-4:every=4 every-5:every=5       1     8          0 -0.3333333
#> 2 every-4:every=4 every-5:every=5       3     4          3         NA
#> 3 every-4:every=4 every-6:every=6       1     8          0 -0.2182179
#> 4 every-4:every=4 every-6:every=6       3     4          4         NA
#> 5 every-5:every=5 every-6:every=6       1     8          0 -0.2182179
#> 6 every-5:every=5 every-6:every=6       3     4          3         NA

Tied shares leave two strata, not three. Stratum “3” holds q01 to q03 and q12, which every-4 and every-6 get wrong as well. In it, one arm of each pair is wrong on all four items (every-5 is right on q12, but its partner is not), so phi there is undefined. The pooled phi then reads only the eight items of stratum “1”, where each arm’s errors fall on items of its own, and it comes out negative.

What a reader keeps: gr_condensation_check()

A reader that carries a running draft through a document, as refine does, condenses as it goes. It can lose an early fact, take a value from a near-namesake, or keep a figure the document later corrected. gr_condensation_check() builds a benchmark that measures each of these without a model judge. In a document (synthetic filler, or a text of your own) it:

  • plants facts, each with a question whose answer is the planted value;
  • plants lures, the same measure for a near-namesake with another value;
  • states one fact wrongly near the start and corrects it near the end.

Each document is given forwards and reversed by paragraph (gr_reverse_text()), so the reverse reader meets first the fact the forward reader meets last.

chk <- gr_condensation_check(n_facts = 4, n_lures = 1, paragraphs = 8)
chk
#> <gr_condensation_check> 1 document(s), forward and reversed, 8 item(s)
#>   per order: 2 fact, 1 lure, 1 correction
chk$items[chk$items$order == "forward", c("kind", "question", "answer", "lure", "superseded")]
#>         kind                                              question answer  lure
#> 1       lure      What was the floor area of the Northgate clinic?  3,565 4,120
#> 2       fact How many yearly visits did the Riverside school have? 10,237  <NA>
#> 3       fact        What was the budget of the Elm Street library?   42.5  <NA>
#> 4 correction       What was the staff count of the Westfield mill?    321  <NA>
#>   superseded
#> 1       <NA>
#> 2       <NA>
#> 3       <NA>
#> 4        264

The two arms below differ in how they carry the document: a running draft or a ledger of findings. Here a stand-in model plays a reader whose draft takes the lure’s value and keeps the superseded figure, while a ledger of findings does neither. On a real model the same code measures what each one does.

facts <- chk$items
condenser <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  text <- vapply(messages, function(m) m$content, "")
  if (grepl("Reply with the edits", text[length(text)], fixed = TRUE)) return("ADD: noted.")
  asks <- text[startsWith(text, "Question: ")]
  row <- facts[facts$question == sub("^Question: ", "", asks[length(asks)]), ][1, ]
  ledger <- any(grepl("<findings>", text, fixed = TRUE))
  if (!ledger && row$kind == "lure") return(paste("It was", row$lure))
  if (!ledger && row$kind == "correction") return(paste("It was", row$superseded))
  paste("It was", row$answer)
})
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("thorough", list(reader = "refine", method = "paragraph")),
                 list(refine_state = c("draft", "ledger")))
cb <- hr_benchmark(arms, chk$reference, runs = 5, client = condenser, scorer = chk$scorer)
gr_condensation_summary(chk, cb)
#>                            arm    order fact_recall lure_rate correction_won
#> 1  thorough:refine_state=draft  forward         0.5         1              0
#> 2  thorough:refine_state=draft reversed         0.5         1              0
#> 3 thorough:refine_state=ledger  forward         1.0         0              1
#> 4 thorough:refine_state=ledger reversed         1.0         0              1
#>   late_recall runs
#> 1         0.5   20
#> 2         0.5   20
#> 3         1.0   20
#> 4         1.0   20

In the summary:

  • fact_recall is the share of runs whose answer holds the planted value;
  • lure_rate is the share of runs on lure items whose answer holds the lure’s;
  • correction_won is the share of runs on the corrected fact that give the new figure and not the old;
  • late_recall is fact recall over the facts in the last third of the document as it was read.

The check’s reference and scorer are ordinary ones, so hr_report() reads the same benchmark with intervals.

Planning the size, and non-inferiority

Often you want to know whether a cheaper arm is worse than the one in use by more than a margin you can live with. That is a non-inferiority test. Whether a benchmark can answer that depends on its size, so check the size before anyone labels 500 questions.

hr_mdd() gives the smallest paired difference a clustered design can detect. It needs the number of items and clusters, the intra-cluster correlation of the paired item difference (ICC_D, taken from a pilot on the dev split) and the share of items on which the arms disagree (p_disc). For 480 questions over 80 documents:

hr_mdd(480, n_clusters = 80, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2)
#> <hr_mdd> 8.2 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.025
#>   480 items in 80 clusters (m = 6, 6 after cv 0), ICC_D 0.2: DE 2, n_eff 240
#>   p_disc 0.2
hr_mdd(480, n_clusters = 80, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2, n_contrasts = 9)
#> <hr_mdd> 10.7 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.002778 (0.025 / 9 contrasts, Holm worst case)
#>   480 items in 80 clusters (m = 6, 6 after cv 0), ICC_D 0.2: DE 2, n_eff 240
#>   p_disc 0.2

Questions in one document count for less than independent ones: the design effect DE = 1 + (m - 1) x ICC_D is 2 here, so 480 questions carry the information of 240. With nine confirmatory contrasts, Holm’s first step tests at 0.025 / 9, and the detectable difference grows from 8.2 to 10.7 points. hr_n_needed() works the other way and gives the items needed for a margin:

hr_n_needed(0.08, m = 6, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2, n_contrasts = 9)
#> <hr_n_needed> 8.0 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.002778 (0.025 / 9 contrasts, Holm worst case)
#>   n_eff 419 effective items; DE 2, so 840 items in 140 clusters of 6

Both use t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom, the ones the report tests with. In the power simulation dev/sim-power.R the formula’s MDD came within 0.25 points of the simulated one. With normal quantiles it fell up to 0.41 points below it at 80 clusters, so both functions use t quantiles.

hr_contrast() states a contrast: the new arm, the reference arm, the margin and whether the new arm must also be cheaper. hr_register_contrasts() fixes the contrasts against the reference before anything scores it. ?hr_contrast suggests a margin of min(0.5 x M1, the loss you would accept in practice), with M1 the reference arm’s advantage over a minimal baseline in a pilot.

hr_register_contrasts() refuses a confirmatory margin below the design’s MDD after Holm, with class hr_margin_below_mdd, since such a margin claims more than the items can show. confirmatory = FALSE registers it as exploratory instead. It also refuses a reference a benchmark has already begun to score, with class hr_registration_after_scoring.

n <- 300
ids <- sprintf("q%03d", 1:n)
docs <- rep(sprintf("doc%02d", 1:50), each = 6)
plan <- hr_reference(ids, labels = rep("yes", n), cluster = docs, split = "test")

design <- hr_mdd(n, n_clusters = 50, icc = 0.1, p_disc = 0.15)
reg <- hr_register_contrasts(plan, hr_contrast("small", "large", margin = 0.10), design)
reg
#> <hr_contrast_registration> 1 contrast(s), 1 confirmatory; registered 2026-11-26T00:56:05.967Z
#>  contrast       label        margin mdd cost_test
#>  small vs large confirmatory 10.0   7.8 yes      
#>   Margins and MDD in points; reference d453122a93af; hash 687fc3f09395

Here the stand-in model finds each item easier or harder by document and by item, and mock-small is a little worse on every one. The governor allows the 3000 calls the benchmark needs:

set.seed(11)
ease <- setNames(rnorm(50, 2, 1)[as.integer(factor(docs))] + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5), ids)
grader <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shift <- if (identical(params$model, "mock-small")) -0.3 else 0
  item <- sub("Item ", "", messages[[1]]$content)
  if (runif(1) < plogis(ease[[item]] + shift)) "yes" else "no"
})

trial <- hr_benchmark(list(ask("large", "mock-large"), ask("small", "mock-small")),
                      plan, runs = 5, client = grader,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 4000, max_cost_usd = 1))
ni <- hr_report(trial, B = 500, registration = reg)
ni$method_reason
#> [1] "300 items in 50 clusters reach 300 items and 30 clusters"
ni$ni[, c("new", "reference", "margin", "estimate", "lower", "cost_upper",
          "verdict", "mdd_design", "mdd_achieved")]
#>     new reference margin    estimate       lower cost_upper verdict mdd_design
#> 1 small     large    0.1 -0.05266667 -0.08118863  -4.32e-05    TRUE 0.07828581
#>   mdd_achieved
#> 1   0.04057211

With 300 items in 50 clusters the report switches to the studentised bootstrap. A contrast holds only if the one-sided lower bound of the accuracy difference is above -margin and, with the cost test, the upper bound of the paired cost difference is below 0.

Here small is 5.3 points less accurate than large. Its lower bound is -8.1 points, inside the margin of 10, and its cost bound is below 0, so the verdict is TRUE. The accuracy bound is the cluster-robust t bound of the paired differences, so at one-sided 0.025 it is the lower end of the printed 95% contrast interval. Confirmatory contrasts are tested with Holm’s step-down procedure. The report prints the design and achieved MDD beside the verdict, with Tango’s paired score interval as a cross-check that does not enter the verdict.

A report with a registration, or with confirmatory = TRUE, is evidence. hr_report() then refuses any row from the dev, exploratory or calibration split with class hr_dev_not_evidence. It refuses a registration edited after it was made too, with class hr_registration_changed.

Judges

Matching text cannot score some answers: a summary, an explanation, an answer that is right in other words. hr_judge() asks a model to choose between candidates ("select"), compare two ("pairwise") or grade one against a reference ("grade"). The model sees the candidates under the letters A, B and so on, never their names, and gets each item in two orders. A verdict that changes with the order, once mapped back to the candidate it names, is "unresolved", never a pick. This stand-in always picks whatever is shown first:

first <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) '{"verdict": "A", "reason": "It is first."}')
j <- hr_judge(c(short = "Revenue was 45.2 million.", long = "Revenue was 51.8 million."),
              first, mode = "select", rubric = "Which candidate gives fiscal 2024 revenue?")
j$outcome
#> [1] "unresolved"
j$verdicts[, c("order", "shown", "verdict", "value")]
#>   order      shown verdict value
#> 1     1 short,long       A short
#> 2     2 long,short       A  long

The judge’s requests pass the same check as hr_call(), under the labels judge.<mode>.o<k>, and go into a trace of the judge’s own. Their cost is in j$judge_cost and never in the trace of the run being judged.

hr_judge_config() holds everything that decides a judge’s answers (model, mode, rubric, the package’s instructions, reply schema, orders, how verdicts are combined, the positive grade) with a hash of it. hr_judge_validate() compares the judge’s decisions with blind human labels for one configuration. It refuses fewer than 50 human-positive or 50 human-negative items, with class hr_judge_too_few_labels, and you cannot lower those minimums. At 10% prevalence, 100 labels hold 10 positives, and sensitivity then has an interval of about plus or minus 0.3. Here the judge’s simulated decisions are right 90% of the time:

hr_register_model("mock-judge", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4)
cfg <- hr_judge_config("mock-judge", "Does the response give the reference's answer?",
                       mode = "grade")

set.seed(3)
human <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(60, 60))
judged <- ifelse(runif(120) < 0.9, human, !human)
judged[c(5, 70)] <- NA       # unresolved by the judge
v <- hr_judge_validate(cfg, data.frame(judge = judged, human = human), B = 200)
v
#> <hr_judge_validation> config e9b61470aa4b (grade, mock-judge)
#>   items: 120 labelled (60 positive, 60 negative), 2 unresolved, 0 dropped
#>   kappa:       0.850 [0.750, 0.950]
#>   sensitivity: 0.933 [0.841, 0.974], n = 60, half-width 0.067
#>   specificity: 0.917 [0.819, 0.964], n = 60
#>   swap inconsistency: 0.017 [0.005, 0.059], 2 of 120

Items the judge left unresolved count as not called positive, as the scorer will count them, so the figures describe the judge as you will use it. Decide before labelling what figures are good enough for your purpose: the function measures the judge and does not approve it. The record is keyed by the configuration’s hash, and hr_judge_valid() tells you when it no longer holds:

hr_judge_valid(v, cfg)
#> [1] TRUE
hr_judge_valid(v, hr_judge_config("mock-judge", "Is the response right?", mode = "grade"))
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"reason")
#> [1] "the judge configuration changed since validation (rubric)"

hr_scorer_judge() is a benchmark scorer that grades each output against its label with a grade-mode judge. Without a valid record it refuses to build (class hr_judge_unvalidated). An unresolved judgement counts as wrong and a failed one as an error, so an arm’s accuracy cannot rise on the items the judge could not settle. The judge’s requests stay in the scorer’s own trace, out of the benchmark’s cost columns:

grader_judge <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shown <- sub(".*Response to grade:", "", messages[[2]]$content)
  ok <- grepl("45.2 million", shown, fixed = TRUE)
  sprintf('{"verdict": "%s", "reason": "Compared."}', if (ok) "pass" else "fail")
})
judge_scorer <- hr_scorer_judge(cfg, v, grader_judge)
judge_scorer$fn("What was revenue?", "It came to 45.2 million dollars.", "45.2 million")$correct
#> [1] TRUE

Accuracy scored by a judge carries the judge’s own errors. hr_judge_ppi() corrects judge-scored accuracy with human labels on a sample, by prediction-powered inference (PPI++ by default). Here a lenient judge passes 30% of wrong answers on 1000 items, and people label 150 of them:

set.seed(7)
truth <- rbinom(1000, 1, 0.6)
lenient <- ifelse(truth == 1, rbinom(1000, 1, 0.95), rbinom(1000, 1, 0.3))
labelled <- rep(NA, 1000)
picked <- sample(1000, 150)
labelled[picked] <- truth[picked]
hr_judge_ppi(lenient, labelled)[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "judge_mean")]
#>    estimate     lower     upper judge_mean
#> 1 0.5668593 0.5053991 0.6283196      0.698
mean(truth)
#> [1] 0.594

The judge alone gives 0.698. Corrected with the 150 labels, the estimate is 0.567, and its interval, 0.505 to 0.628, holds the true share of 0.594. If the labelled items were drawn with unequal probabilities, pass inclusion_prob and the correction is inverse probability weighted. The interval is a normal approximation and runs narrow with few labels at small inclusion probabilities.

Checks that run a program

Besides a label or a judge, a benchmark can score what a program says about an output. hr_step_command() builds a step that runs one program you name, such as Rscript on a test file, and reads its result as "passed" or "failed". Put it in a chain (see vignette("compose")) after the step that writes what it checks.

The step runs the program with your own privileges, through system2(). Each element of argv is one argument, never split on spaces. There is no default command, and the step never takes a command from a model’s reply. The API key is unset for the call, and the program inherits the rest of the environment. A command step sends no request, so it adds no cost.

The examples below run the R that builds this guide, so they work offline. The draft step writes a small R file for each item in place of a model’s draft, and the check runs it:

rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")
tasks <- hr_reference(list(t1 = "1 + 1 == 2", t2 = "1 + 1 == 3"),
                      labels = c("passed", "failed"), cluster = c("a", "b"),
                      split = "test")
draft <- hr_step("draft", function(input, ctx) {
  f <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
  writeLines(sprintf("stopifnot(%s)", input), f)
  list(file = f)
})
run_file <- function(input, ctx) c(rscript, input$file)
status_is <- hr_scorer(function(item, output, label) {
  held <- attr(output, "hr_held")$check
  s <- if (is.null(held)) output$check$status else held$status
  list(correct = identical(s, label), outcome = s, failure_kind = NA)
}, name = "status")

The scorer reads a held result from attr(output, "hr_held") and a visible one from output$check, so it scores a chain either way.

How long a command may run

What it controls. timeout is the number of seconds the program may run before it is stopped. A program stopped at the limit gets the status "timeout" and the degradation "command_timeout", and counts as neither passed nor failed. The step ends the program, but processes it started in the background (or that ignore the signal) can keep running on any platform. On Windows, any process it started can keep running.

Signs it needs changing. Runs whose status is "timeout" on items that pass when run by hand (the limit is too short for the machine), or a benchmark that takes far longer than its checks should (a stuck program is waiting out a long limit).

Where the default came from. Sixty seconds, enough for a small test file, set when the step was written and not tuned. It is untested.

How to test it. Sweep it by path. Each value changes the configuration, so each value is its own arm. Here both values are long enough, and the outcomes agree:

chain <- hr_chain(draft = draft,
                  check = hr_step_command("check", run_file, held = TRUE),
                  name = "checked")
arms <- hr_sweep(chain, data.frame(check.timeout = c(5, 60)))
tb <- hr_benchmark(arms, tasks, runs = 5, client = NULL, scorer = status_is)
table(tb$arm, tb$outcome)
#>                           
#>                            failed passed
#>   checked:check.timeout=5       5      5
#>   checked:check.timeout=60      5      5

How the result is read

What it controls. parse = "exit" reads the exit code: 0 is "passed", anything else "failed". parse = "testthat" reads the last [ FAIL n | WARN n | SKIP n | PASS n ] line the program printed: "failed" when FAIL is above 0, and "error" when there is no such line. For testthat the exit code alone falls short, because testthat::test_file() exits with 0 when a test fails unless you give it stop_on_failure = TRUE.

Signs it needs changing. A check that runs a test file and reports "passed" for drafts that fail their tests: it is reading the exit code of a run that does not stop on failure. With "testthat", a status of "error" on every run means the program prints no summary line, so the command is not running the tests.

Where the default came from. "exit" reads what every program reports. It was chosen, never tuned, and is untested.

How to test it. Run the same test file both ways. Without stop_on_failure = TRUE the exit code is 0, so "exit" passes what "testthat" fails:

tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
writeLines("testthat::test_that('sum', testthat::expect_equal(1 + 1, 3))", tf)
quiet <- function(input, ctx) {
  c(rscript, "-e", sprintf("testthat::test_file('%s')", gsub("\\\\", "/", tf)))
}
one <- hr_reference(list(t1 = "sum"), labels = "failed", cluster = "a", split = "test")
tests <- hr_chain(draft = hr_step("draft", function(input, ctx) list()),
                  check = hr_step_command("check", quiet, held = TRUE),
                  name = "tests")
pb <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(tests, data.frame(check.parse = c("exit", "testthat"))),
                   one, runs = 5, client = NULL, scorer = status_is)
table(pb$arm, pb$outcome)
#>                             
#>                              error passed
#>   tests:check.parse=exit         0      5
#>   tests:check.parse=testthat     5      0

Whether later steps see the result

What it controls. With held = FALSE the step returns its input with the result in $check, so a later step (a revise step, say) can read it. With held = TRUE the step passes its input on unchanged, records the status as the signal "command.<step>", and attaches the result as attr(output, "hr_held") for the scorer. A held step must come last in its chain: hr_chain() refuses a step that is not held after one that is.

Signs it needs changing. A chain whose revise step sees the check that scores it. The check then becomes a target for the revise step, and its pass rate says little about drafts the check never saw. Hold that check back, and use a separate visible check for the revise step.

Where the default came from. Off, so the steps after it see the result. It was chosen for the chain, never tuned, and is untested.

How to test it. Sweep it on the last step. The outcomes agree, since nothing after the check reads it, but only the held arm records the signal:

hs <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(chain, data.frame(check.held = c(FALSE, TRUE))), tasks,
                   runs = 5, client = NULL, scorer = status_is)
table(hs$arm, hs$outcome)
#>                           
#>                            failed passed
#>   checked:check.held=FALSE      5      5
#>   checked:check.held=TRUE       5      5
table(hr_signals(hs)$arm)
#> 
#> checked:check.held=TRUE 
#>                      10

The difference shows when a step comes after the check. Here a visible check feeds a revise step that fixes any draft that failed, and a held check scores the result:

revise <- hr_step("revise", function(input, ctx) {
  if (identical(input$check$status, "failed")) writeLines("stopifnot(TRUE)", input$file)
  input
})
both <- hr_chain(draft = draft,
                 look = hr_step_command("look", run_file),
                 revise = revise,
                 check = hr_step_command("check", run_file, held = TRUE),
                 name = "revised")
hb <- hr_benchmark(list(chain, both), tasks, runs = 5, client = NULL,
                   scorer = status_is)
table(hb$arm, hb$outcome)
#>          
#>           failed passed
#>   checked      5      5
#>   revised      0     10
hr_signals(hb)[1:3, c("arm", "item", "signal", "value")]
#>       arm item        signal  value
#> 1 checked   t1 command.check passed
#> 2 checked   t1 command.check passed
#> 3 checked   t1 command.check passed
unlink(tf)

The revised chain passes every draft, so it is scored wrong on t2, whose label says the draft should fail. A command step checks only what its command checks, and the package never chooses the command.

Baselines without a model

A configuration that calls a model should beat one that does not. hr_baseline_classifier() fits a ridge logistic regression on tf-idf features (hr_tfidf()) and cross-fits it, so a model that never saw an item predicts it, with the vocabulary fitted on each training fold only. Folds are stratified by label, or keep each cluster whole:

set.seed(1)
words <- function(pool, n) vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(pool, 6, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")
abstracts <- c(words(c("masks", "infection", "trial", "ward", "virus"), 10),
               words(c("budget", "policy", "school", "survey", "income"), 50))
relevant <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(10, 50))

hr_baseline_classifier(abstracts, relevant, folds = 5)
#> <hr_baseline_classifier> ridge logistic, 2 labels, 5 folds
#>   accuracy: 1.000 [0.940, 1.000], 60 of 60 out of fold
#>   training size per fold: 48, 48, 48, 48, 48

Real abstracts do not separate this cleanly. Run the baseline on the same labelled set as the model screener: a screener no more accurate than it costs calls and buys nothing.

hr_baseline_ranker() simulates prioritised screening over a set whose relevance is known, as ASReview’s simulation mode does: it starts from one relevant and one irrelevant record, refits after each batch, and screens the record with the highest predicted relevance next. It reports the records screened to reach 95% recall and WSS@95, the share left unread at that recall less the 5% a random order would leave:

ranked <- hr_baseline_ranker(abstracts, relevant)
ranked
#> <hr_baseline_ranker> logistic, 60 records, 10 relevant, 9 fits
#>   95% recall after 11 records (random order: 55.5 expected)
#>   WSS@95: 0.767

gr_stop_test() takes this result, or any screening order, and says when prioritised screening may stop; vignette("review") covers it.

Drift

A provider can change a model behind the same name. hr_drift_check() reruns an arm live on the items of a frozen benchmark and compares the two item by item. You fix alpha and an optional alert in the call, before anything is rerun. Here the model now gets two capitals wrong:

six <- hr_reference(
  items = list(q1 = "France", q2 = "Peru", q3 = "Chad", q4 = "Fiji", q5 = "Chile", q6 = "Laos"),
  labels = c("Paris", "Lima", "N'Djamena", "Suva", "Santiago", "Vientiane"),
  cluster = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"), split = "test")
then <- c(France = "Paris", Peru = "Lima", Chad = "N'Djamena", Fiji = "Suva",
          Chile = "Santiago", Laos = "Vientiane")
now <- then
now[c("Chad", "Laos")] <- c("Ndjamena", "Luang Prabang")
answers <- function(table) {
  hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) table[[sub("Capital of ", "", messages[[1]]$content)]])
}

frozen <- hr_benchmark(capital, six, runs = 5, client = answers(then))
drift <- hr_drift_check(frozen, capital, client = answers(now), reference = six,
                        alert = 0.1, B = 500)
drift
#> <hr_drift_check> arm 'capital': 5 frozen run(s) vs 5 live, 6 item(s) in 3 cluster(s); alpha 0.05
#> (a) Accuracy: frozen 1.000, live 0.667, change -0.333 [-0.500, -0.167], p 0.0122; changed: yes
#>     Clustered McNemar (Obuchowski): X^2 4.000, p 0.0455; agrees: yes
#> (b) Flips: between frozen runs 0.000, between live runs 0.000, frozen vs live 0.333, excess 0.333 (one-sided lower 0.000), p 0.333; in excess: no
#>     Frozen pairs flip 0.000 to 0.000; frozen-live pairs 0.333 to 0.333
#> Drift: yes; alert at 0.100: crossed
#> Items: lost 2, gained 0, worse 0, better 0, same 4 
#>  item cluster change frozen live  frozen_outcome live_outcome 
#>  q3   b       lost   1.000  0.000 n'djamena      ndjamena     
#>  q6   c       lost   1.000  0.000 vientiane      luang prabang
#> Note: 6 items in 3 clusters fall short of 300 items and 30 clusters, where the cluster bootstrap can undercover; read the tests as approximate.

Test (a) is the change in accuracy, live minus frozen, by a cluster bootstrap over documents, with the clustered McNemar test beside it. Test (b) checks whether frozen and live runs disagree more than replicate runs disagree among themselves. Per item it estimates the squared change, so it also catches losses and gains that cancel in accuracy.

Here (a) finds the two lost items: a change of -0.333 with an interval that lies wholly beyond the alert of 0.1. Test (b) does not reject, since with three clusters its one-sided bound reaches 0. The live rerun is in drift$live, an hr_bench you can report or keep as the next frozen sample.

hr_drift_check() refuses fewer than 5 frozen runs, a changed arm, another reference or scorer, and a live rerun answered from a cache or a recording. That last one would return the frozen reply again instead of the model’s answer today.

Signals, calibration and gate thresholds

Some readers report on their own work: the iterative reader says at each step whether it can answer, preview says which sections its plan would skip, and ensemble says how it settled its members. hr_signal() records such a value as a local step in the trace. That step sends no request and changes no cache key. hr_signals() reads the values back:

reader <- hr_mock_client(function(m, p) {
  '{"can_answer": true, "answer": "45.2 million dollars", "next_query": ""}'
})
ch <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150))
read <- gr_read(ch, "What was revenue?", reader, "iterative")
hr_signals(read)[, c("signal", "value", "score", "refs")]
#>                    signal value score        refs
#> 1 gr.iterative.can_answer  TRUE     1 {"round":1}

A signal is advisory. Nothing in the package acts on one, and a signal may gate an action only after you measure it against items whose right answer is known. hr_calibrate_signal() takes that measure on a graded set, which must include unanswerable items. A signal measured only on answerable questions has never been tested on the case where “I can answer” is most often wrong.

hr_calibrate_signal() fits a map from the signal to a probability on half of each cluster’s items and measures it on the other half. It reports the Brier score, type-2 AUROC, the area under the risk-coverage curve and a debiased calibration error, each with a cluster bootstrap interval. The record is keyed by the served model, its version, the task, format, prompt hash, effort, module and contract version. The graded set here is simulated, 1200 items in 120 documents:

set.seed(2)
n <- 1200
answerable <- runif(n) < 0.8
score <- runif(n) * ifelse(answerable, 1, 0.6)
graded <- data.frame(cluster = rep(sprintf("doc%03d", 1:120), each = 10),
                     score = score, answerable = answerable,
                     correct = runif(n) < plogis(-6 + 12 * score) / ifelse(answerable, 1, 3))
key <- list(served_model = "mock-large-2026-01", version = "2026-01", task = "qa",
            format = "txt", prompt_hash = "a1b2c3", effort = NA, module = "iterative")

cal <- hr_calibrate_signal("gr.iterative.can_answer", graded, key, seed = 3, B = 200)
cal
#> <hr_calibration> gr.iterative.can_answer: advisory
#>   1200 items (715 wrong, 266 unanswerable) in 120 clusters; map: platt
#>   key: served_model=mock-large-2026-01, version=2026-01, task=qa, format=txt, prompt_hash=a1b2c3, effort=NA, module=iterative, contract_version=0.1
#>   calibration half: 600 items, accuracy 0.400
#>   brier   0.0914  [0.0761, 0.1075]
#>   auroc2  0.9454  [0.9282, 0.9619]
#>   aurc    0.2677  [0.2358, 0.3110]
#>   ece     0.0695  [0.0264, 0.1021]
#>   advisory: no gate threshold has been set

A new record is always advisory. hr_gate_threshold() uses Learn-then-Test to find the loosest threshold at which acting on the items at or above it keeps a risk below alpha with confidence 1 - delta. It tests thresholds from strict to loose with a one-sided Clopper-Pearson bound and stops at the first that fails. Errors from one document go together, so the bound is taken on an effective number of items, n / deff, where the design effect deff is measured over the calibration half’s clusters at each threshold. alpha has no default, since you set it for the task:

cal <- hr_gate_threshold(cal, "stop", alpha = 0.1)
as.data.frame(cal$gate[c("threshold", "n", "k", "deff", "ucb", "coverage", "status")])
#>   threshold   n k     deff        ucb coverage status
#> 1 0.8510243 147 7 1.258159 0.09408169    0.245 passed
cal$status
#> [1] "gating"

At the threshold kept, 147 items of the calibration half are acted on, 7 of them wrongly. The design effect is 1.26, so the bound counts them as about 117 independent items, and the upper bound on the error among them is 0.094 (0.088 if the items were independent).

A record becomes "gating" only when it has all four of these:

  • a passing threshold;
  • at least 100 wrong items in the graded set;
  • a map that rises with the signal;
  • a calibration error over at least 5 bins.

Items with the same p share a bin, so a signal with fewer than 5 values, such as a logical one, stays advisory. A graded set with a split column, as hr_assign_splits() gives, is calibrated on its calibration rows alone. Even with a gating record, the signal gates only through a policy, and only for a run whose key matches the record:

policy <- hr_signal_policy("gr.iterative.can_answer", "stop")
hr_apply_signal(c(0.95, 0.4), policy, cal, key)[, c("value", "p", "gated", "act", "route")]
#>   value         p gated   act       route
#> 1  0.95 0.9938152  TRUE  TRUE         act
#> 2   0.4 0.1982915  TRUE FALSE route_check

later <- utils::modifyList(key, list(served_model = "mock-large-2026-06"))
hr_calibration_valid(cal, later)
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"differs")
#> [1] "served_model"
hr_apply_signal(0.95, policy, cal, later)$reason
#> [1] "the record does not hold for this run (served_model differs)"

If the signal cannot gate, on_fail routes the item: to a check (the default), to a person, or nowhere. No reader calls hr_apply_signal() yet, so in this release nothing gates on a signal.

The statistics underneath

The functions above rest on five that you can also use on their own.

hr_prop_ci() gives Wilson, Clopper-Pearson or Jeffreys intervals for a proportion. Use Wilson for a descriptive rate and Clopper-Pearson for an “at least” or “at most” claim, read as a one-sided bound:

hr_prop_ci(46, 50)[, c("est", "lower", "upper", "method")]
#>    est     lower     upper method
#> 1 0.92 0.8116175 0.9684505 wilson
hr_prop_ci(46, 50, method = "clopper_pearson", side = "lower")[, c("lower", "method", "side")]
#>       lower          method  side
#> 1 0.8262088 clopper_pearson lower

hr_agreement() reports agreement between two raters as the count table with observed agreement, Cohen’s kappa with a bootstrap interval, the prevalence and bias indices, PABAK, Gwet’s AC1, and sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV when positive is given. Kappa is never reported alone, since it moves with prevalence as much as with agreement. For a matrix of coders, or an ordinal, interval or ratio level, it reports Krippendorff’s alpha instead. Below 30 items that can be paired, alpha is NA and only percent agreement is reported.

screener <- rep(c("keep", "drop", "keep", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
person   <- rep(c("keep", "keep", "drop", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
hr_agreement(screener, person, positive = "keep", B = 200)$stats[1:4, ]
#>            statistic  estimate        se     lower     upper
#> 1 observed agreement 0.8500000        NA 0.7671644 0.9069401
#> 2              kappa 0.6995192 0.0713936 0.5620888 0.8377657
#> 3              PABAK 0.7000000        NA 0.5343288 0.8138803
#> 4                AC1 0.7007481 0.0713518 0.5591707 0.8423256

hr_ht_estimate() estimates a total, a mean or a ratio from a sample drawn with known inclusion probabilities, optionally by stratum. Screening recall on a stacked reference is weighted with it. hr_ppi() is the prediction-powered estimate behind hr_judge_ppi(). hr_alt_test() runs the alternative annotator test of Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025), which tests whether a model’s labels can stand in for those of three or more people, with the margin set by the people’s declared expertise (expertise has no default):

set.seed(3)
gold <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, replace = TRUE)
noisy <- function(p) ifelse(runif(80) < p, gold, sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, TRUE))
people <- sapply(1:4, function(j) noisy(0.75))
alt <- hr_alt_test(noisy(0.95), people, expertise = "skilled")
alt$omega
#> [1] 1
alt$passed
#> [1] TRUE

The model here wins against each of the four annotators, so the winning rate omega is 1 and the test passes. The test needs at least 30 items with two or more human labels, and hr_alt_test() warns below 50.
